patients.label: Girl with overlapping ASD and SLI symptoms, 36 months at admission, followed to 66 months

identity_evidence.quote: The girl is the only child of young (mother 30 years, father 32 years), healthy, non-consanguineous parents.

attribution_limitations: Table A1 caption describes the theta values as measured during auditory-verbal processing, but the table rows are labelled RS (resting state) and LT (listening task).

Table 1 prints VIQ and PIQ at all six time points, but the methods say REVISK was applied only at t4 and t5 and RTČ-P (coefficient of mental development) earlier; the instrument behind each VIQ/PIQ cell is not stated.
The RTČ-P sentence lists four points (t0, t1, t2 and t3) while calling them the first three assessment points.
Follow-up is described as two and a half years of therapy (36 to 66 months) in the introduction and conclusions but as a two-year treatment follow-up in the discussion.
The discussion names left (F1, F3, F7) and right (F2, F4, F8) frontal electrodes, whereas Table A2 and the electrode list use Fp1/Fp2 with F3, F4, F7, F8.
The sensory-profile discussion says capacities stabilize at points t3 to t6, but only t0 to t5 exist.
The text calls t1 the first assessment point and says the initial assessment was at t0, the starting time point.
It was hard to distinguish whether the speech and language deficit was an independent disorder or part of ASD at first admission.

Table 5 prints a normalized GARS value of 0.98 at t1, whereas the described scaling of the Table 2 autism index (subtract 52, divide by 74) gives 0.959 for the printed index of 123. Table 5 and Table 6 are author-derived rescalings and correlations and are not recorded as observations.
The SEPAC ESLD row prints numbers without a unit.
The case report says integrative therapy began immediately after the examination, whereas the study design says treatment started seven days after the initial evaluation.
The working diagnosis is ASD with overlapping SLI symptoms, but the team states it was hard to determine with certainty whether the child had ASD or SLI.

evidence.quote:
Figure 1
Comparison of the normalized achievement in all evaluation tests in all assessment points. Note: SP—sensory profile; GARS—Gilliam Autism Rating Scale; EEG—electroencephalography; SLD—speech–language development; VIQ—verbal IQ; PIQ—performance IQ.

limitations: Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; the one JPEG is inspected in the separate visual target.

Table 5 (normalized values) and Table 6 (correlations) are author-derived rescalings and statistics over six time points; they are not recorded as observations. Table A2 Frange and Fnorm are likewise rescalings; only Fdiff is recorded.

GARS-3 subscale NA cells (cognitive style, maladaptive speech at t0 to t2) and CCC-2 NA cells (t0, t1) and the t5 degree-of-difficulty slash are not-assigned cells with no result; they are not recorded as facts.
Table 3 Visual SD at t2 is printed as a slash and no SD category is recorded for it.
Instruments behind Table 1 VIQ/PIQ cells and the unit of SEPAC ESLD are not stated; none inferred.
Statistical analyses (no significant theta change per electrode, correlations, 20 percent change) are analysis conclusions, not recorded as patient observations.
Discussion comparisons with literature and cited studies are background and not patient facts.

Table 5 normalized values, Table 6 correlations and Table A2 Frange/Fnorm are author rescalings or statistics of values already recorded as observations; they appear only as derived series in the measurement-series sidecar.

case_context.index_subject_description: Girl with overlapping autism spectrum disorder and specific language impairment symptoms, followed from 36 to 66 months of age
case_context.care_setting: Institute for experimental phonetics and speech pathology (IEPSP), Belgrade, Serbia

evidence.quote: we report the autism risk index and cognitive, speech–language, and sensory profile of a girl with overlapping ASD and SLI symptoms in a prospective, longitudinal study between 36 and 66 months of age
A multidisciplinary admission team examined the child at the institute for experimental phonetics and speech pathology (IEPSP) in Belgrade, Serbia.
She was 36 months old when her parents brought her for an examination
The girl is the only child of young
She lives in a monolingual family where the Serbian language is spoken.

claims.text: A girl, the only child of healthy non-consanguineous parents, was born at 40 weeks after a normal pregnancy and uncomplicated delivery, with normal hearing on screening and BERA. Social withdrawal and behavioural manifestations began around 18 months. At 36 months she was non-verbal, uncooperative, avoided eye contact, did not respond to her name, showed repetitive movements and stereotypies, and had severe receptive and expressive language deficits.

evidence.quote: we report the autism risk index and cognitive, speech–language, and sensory profile of a girl with overlapping ASD and SLI symptoms in a prospective, longitudinal study between 36 and 66 months of age
A multidisciplinary admission team examined the child at the institute for experimental phonetics and speech pathology (IEPSP) in Belgrade, Serbia.
She was 36 months old when her parents brought her for an examination
The girl is the only child of young
She lives in a monolingual family where the Serbian language is spoken.
At the time of admission, the child was non-verbal (without functional words), uncooperative, and manifesting ASD symptoms.
she showed a distinct level of excitement and irritability in the presence of strangers
walked from wall to wall of the room
did not react to her parents’ attempt to calm her down
She did not accept any toys, not even manipulative ones.
It was not possible to direct her to a specific activity or game.
She often pulled her mother’s hand to go outside.
She expressed a tendency to avoid eye contact
she showed atypical responses to eye gaze
She did not respond to her name when called by her parents or others.
Gradual “exclusion” from the social environment and behavioral specific manifestations began to manifest around 18 months.
there was no interaction between the girl and the therapist during joint play with toys or some other activities
She did not initiate or share joint attention.
she did not use or understand demonstrative gestures (pointing, showing, and giving)
Compensatory use of non-verbal communication was missing
She used her parent’s hand to achieve the desired goal.
Social interaction with examiners was extremely poor.
she had restricted behavior and play; she often visually explored toys
She manifested repetitive body movements like hand flapping and constantly moving around the room.
The sensory profile manifested as disgust for specific textures and selecting some foods by color.
There was no adequate reaction and localization of low- or high-frequency sounds in space, even when they were of high intensity when she was in an activity.
She showed reactions more strongly to particular auditory and visual effects from TV content (commercials, cartoons).

Speech comprehension was markedly reduced. The girl barely understood the speech of her parents and the environment, and her understanding was at the level of a few simple experiential tasks that were situationally supported.
Her reaction to a verbal order was faster and more reliable for simple, situational, verbal orders from the immediate social environment if they were related to her own need or current interest.
She did not produce any functional words or holophrases during the first assessment.
she used her central voice production and babbling without communicative function
the girl had severe receptive and expressive language deficits, and fell significantly behind the chronological age considering speech–language development
the functional use of objects and toys was minimal; she took toys, looked at them briefly, and threw them without imitation of movement and play
the lingual phase was inconsistent after the babbling phase
Her motor development was typical (sitting at seven months, walking at 12 months).
She used her right hand more often at admission
A hearing assessment performed using the brain-stem-evoked response audiometry (BERA) showed normal auditory function at the level of 20 db bilaterally.
Hearing screening tests indicated normal hearing.
She was born at 40 weeks of gestation after a normal pregnancy.
Pre- or perinatal risk factors were not present.
Specific family heredity did not exist.
The problem deepened by going to kindergarten around the age of two.
Her mother and father calmed her down with difficulty.
According to the parents, she would react similarly in an unknown environment and in a familiar one, e.g., with grandparents who lived one floor below their apartment.

claims.text: A multidisciplinary admission team at an institute in Belgrade made a working diagnosis of ASD with overlapping SLI symptoms, noting that certainty was hard to reach because she was 36 months old and had not been treated before. Treatment began after the initial evaluation. Behavioural, cognitive, autism, sensory and speech-language instruments and EEG at rest and during auditory-verbal stimulation were repeated every six months from 36 to 66 months.

claims.text: Integrative therapy comprised speech-language therapy, sensory integration, psychomotor re-education and counseling sessions for the mother. The child showed no progress in the first six months, behavioural retests changed minimally and only EEG findings differed. Receptive and expressive language progress was noticed at 48 months, and at 54 months she was verbal with functional agrammatical speech.

source_evidence.quote: we report the autism risk index and cognitive, speech–language, and sensory profile of a girl with overlapping ASD and SLI symptoms in a prospective, longitudinal study between 36 and 66 months of age
A multidisciplinary admission team examined the child at the institute for experimental phonetics and speech pathology (IEPSP) in Belgrade, Serbia.
She was 36 months old when her parents brought her for an examination
The girl is the only child of young
She lives in a monolingual family where the Serbian language is spoken.
the multidisciplinary admission team made the so-called working diagnosis: ASD and overlapping SLI symptoms
it was hard to determine with certainty whether the child had ASD or SLI
the multidisciplinary admission team made the so-called working diagnosis: ASD and overlapping SLI symptoms
it was hard to determine with certainty whether the child had ASD or SLI
At the time of admission, the child was non-verbal (without functional words), uncooperative, and manifesting ASD symptoms.
At the time of admission, the child was non-verbal (without functional words), uncooperative, and manifesting ASD symptoms.
At the time of admission, the child was non-verbal (without functional words), uncooperative, and manifesting ASD symptoms.
she showed a distinct level of excitement and irritability in the presence of strangers
walked from wall to wall of the room
did not react to her parents’ attempt to calm her down
She did not accept any toys, not even manipulative ones.
It was not possible to direct her to a specific activity or game.
She often pulled her mother’s hand to go outside.
She expressed a tendency to avoid eye contact
she showed atypical responses to eye gaze
She did not respond to her name when called by her parents or others.
Gradual “exclusion” from the social environment and behavioral specific manifestations began to manifest around 18 months.
there was no interaction between the girl and the therapist during joint play with toys or some other activities
She did not initiate or share joint attention.
she did not use or understand demonstrative gestures (pointing, showing, and giving)
Compensatory use of non-verbal communication was missing
She used her parent’s hand to achieve the desired goal.
Social interaction with examiners was extremely poor.
she had restricted behavior and play; she often visually explored toys
She manifested repetitive body movements like hand flapping and constantly moving around the room.
The sensory profile manifested as disgust for specific textures and selecting some foods by color.
The sensory profile manifested as disgust for specific textures and selecting some foods by color.
There was no adequate reaction and localization of low- or high-frequency sounds in space, even when they were of high intensity when she was in an activity.
She showed reactions more strongly to particular auditory and visual effects from TV content (commercials, cartoons).

Speech comprehension was markedly reduced. The girl barely understood the speech of her parents and the environment, and her understanding was at the level of a few simple experiential tasks that were situationally supported.
Her reaction to a verbal order was faster and more reliable for simple, situational, verbal orders from the immediate social environment if they were related to her own need or current interest.
She did not produce any functional words or holophrases during the first assessment.
she used her central voice production and babbling without communicative function
the girl had severe receptive and expressive language deficits, and fell significantly behind the chronological age considering speech–language development
the functional use of objects and toys was minimal; she took toys, looked at them briefly, and threw them without imitation of movement and play
the lingual phase was inconsistent after the babbling phase
Her motor development was typical (sitting at seven months, walking at 12 months).
She used her right hand more often at admission
was confirmed to be right-handed at an older age
She was inconsolable with the presence of crying and anger, refusing any contact with the tendency to widen that gap even more.
at the beginning (time point t0), the child’s sensory processing significantly deviated from the norm
At the last time point (t5), the girl’s sensory processing was like in typically developing children on most subscales.
At 54 months, the child was verbal using functional agrammatical speech. She expressed her needs verbally and communicated with people from the environment.
Her speech–language ability was further improved at 60 and 66 months, although reduced in particular segments of grammar and vocabulary.
At these two assessment points (60 and 66 months of age), the girl was verbal and had developed speech–language abilities.
